chapter.name: Cell: The Building Block of Life

questions.q: Sunita fits a 10X eyepiece and a 40X objective lens to her school microscope and studies an onion cell whose estimated size is 200 µm. Under this set-up the cell appears ___ times larger.
In Activity 2.1, Imran measures the diameter of the field of view as 3.2 mm and counts 16 onion peel cells in one straight line along that diameter. Which estimate of the size of one cell is correct?
questions.a: 200 µm. The diameter is first converted, 3.2 mm = 3200 µm, and 3200 µm divided by 16 cells gives 200 µm.
o: 200 µm
0.2 µm
20 µm

questions.q: Ritu draws two dots on paper 0.08 mm apart and views them from 25 cm without any lens. What does she see?
questions.a: A single point, because the gap is below the eye's limit of resolution. At the near point the eye separates two points only if they are about 0.1 mm apart or more.
o: A single point, because the gap is below the eye's limit of resolution
Two faint dots, because the eye can separate points once they are less than 1 mm apart
Two separate dots, because 0.08 mm is close enough to the 0.1 mm limit of resolution
Two separate dots, because any gap above zero can be seen by the eye at 25 cm

questions.q: Arjun first views a cell through a 10X eyepiece and a 10X objective, then switches to a 40X objective with the same eyepiece. Compared with the first view, the cell now appears
questions.a: 4 times larger than before. Total magnification rises from 100X to 400X, and 400 divided by 100 is 4.
o: 4 times larger than before
40 times larger than before
10 times larger than before
400 times larger than before

questions.q: A slide shows a cell whose nucleus and cytoplasm look equally grey, so the two parts cannot be told apart even though the image is large. Which of the three features that scientists improved in microscopes will help most here?
questions.a: Contrast, the difference in brightness between parts of an object. Parts that look equally bright need contrast; making the image bigger does not change their brightness.
o: Contrast, the difference in brightness between parts of an object
Magnification, the number of times the image is enlarged compared with the object
Resolution, the ability to see two close points as separate and distinct
The limit of resolution of the unaided eye, which is 0.1 mm at 25 cm

questions.q: A student says the plasma membrane of a cell is about 5 nm thick. Written in metres, 5 nm is
questions.a: 5 × 10⁻⁹ m. A nanometre is one-billionth of a metre, so 5 nm = 5 × 10⁻⁹ m.

questions.q:
Read the statements about microscopes.
Statement 1: Resolution is a measure of how clearly two close points are seen as separate and distinct in the image.
Statement 2: Contrast is the difference in brightness between various parts of an object.
Statement 3: An electron microscope forms its image with a beam of light of a very short wavelength.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only. The first two match the book. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons instead of light, so the third is false.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 only
1, 2 and 3
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A microscope with a 10X eyepiece and a 10X objective makes a cell of estimated size 200 µm appear 100 times larger.
Reason (R): The total magnification of a microscope is the sum of the magnifying powers of the eyepiece and the objective lens.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. A is true, since 10 × 10 = 100. R is false, because the powers are multiplied, not added (10 + 10 would give only 20).
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
A student finds the diameter of the visible field to be 2.7 mm and counts 18 onion peel cells along it. Her microscope has a 10X eyepiece and a 15X objective.
(a) Estimate the size of one cell in µm.
(b) How large, in mm, does one cell appear through this microscope?
questions.a: (a) 2.7 mm = 2700 µm, and 2700/18 = 150 µm. (b) Total magnification = 10 × 15 = 150X, so the cell appears 150 × 150 µm = 22 500 µm = 22.5 mm.
s: Part (a): converts to µm and divides by the cell count to get 150 µm
Part (b): multiplies the powers to get 150X and applies it to 150 µm to get 22.5 mm

questions.q:
Two pairs of dots are drawn on paper held at the near point of the eye: pair P is 0.3 mm apart and pair Q is 0.07 mm apart.
(a) Which pair is seen as two distinct dots by the unaided eye?
(b) What would you use to see pair Q as two dots, and why does it work?
questions.a: (a) Pair P, because 0.3 mm is more than the limit of resolution of 0.1 mm. (b) A convex lens (or a combination of lenses), which magnifies the object so that the gap appears larger than the eye's limit of resolution.
s: Part (a): pair P, with the 0.1 mm limit as the reason
Part (b): a convex lens or lens combination that magnifies the gap

questions.q: Differentiate between magnification and resolution of a microscope, using one line for each.
questions.a: Magnification tells how many times larger the image appears than the object (for example 100X). Resolution is the measure of clarity, that is, how well two close points are seen as separate and distinct.
s: Magnification: how many times the image is enlarged
Resolution: clarity, close points seen as separate

questions.q: Neha says, 'Robert Hooke's microscope showed cork cells, so it must have shown mitochondria and ribosomes too.' Judge her statement using the magnification Hooke's microscope had and what the chapter says about organelles.
questions.a: Not supported. Hooke's microscope gave only about 200-300X, enough to see the box-like compartments he named cells. The chapter says most organelles are visible only with an electron microscope, which works at the nanometre scale.
s: Judgement: not supported, with Hooke's 200-300X microscope
Reason: most organelles need an electron microscope (nanometre scale)

questions.q:
The limit of resolution of the human eye is 0.1 mm.
(a) Express it in µm.
(b) How many bacteria, each 2 µm across, placed side by side would just fill a length equal to this limit?
questions.a: (a) 0.1 mm = 0.1 × 1000 = 100 µm. (b) 100 µm divided by 2 µm = 50 bacteria.
s: Part (a): 100 µm using 1 mm = 1000 µm
Part (b): 100/2 = 50 bacteria

questions.q: Farhan claims, 'The higher the magnification of a microscope, the clearer the cell always looks.' Is the claim right? Explain using the features that scientists have improved in microscopes.
questions.a: Partly right. Higher magnification does make the cell appear larger, but clarity also depends on resolution (the measure of clarity) and contrast (the difference in brightness between parts). Scientists improved all three features, so a big but blurred image is not a clearer one.
s: Verdict: partly right, magnification enlarges the image
Names resolution (clarity) and contrast (brightness difference) as the other features
Concludes a large image can still be unclear

questions.q: Divya measures the diameter of the field as 4 mm, counts 20 cells along it, and reports the cell size as 4/20 = 0.2 µm. Show that this size is impossible for an onion peel cell and find her error.
questions.a: Her answer is not possible because 0.2 µm is far smaller than even a typical bacterial cell (1-10 µm), and an onion cell is eukaryotic, typically 10-100 µm. Her error is that she did not convert 4 mm into µm. Correctly 4 mm = 4000 µm and 4000/20 = 200 µm.
s: Shows 0.2 µm is below even the 1-10 µm of a bacterium
Identifies the missing conversion from mm to µm
Corrects the working to 4000/20 = 200 µm

questions.q: Write a situation for Activity 2.1 in which the field of view is 6 mm wide and the estimated size of the onion peel cell comes out as 200 µm. State how many cells must have been counted and show the working.
questions.a: The ruler shows a field diameter of 6 mm = 6000 µm. For an estimate of 200 µm, the student must count 6000/200 = 30 cells along the diameter in a straight line.
s: Field diameter 6 mm converted to 6000 µm
Number of cells found as 6000/200
Answer of 30 cells, counted along the diameter in one line

questions.q:
Three groups did Activity 2.1 on the same onion peel. Group P: field 5 mm, 25 cells. Group Q: field 5 mm, 20 cells. Group R: field 4 mm, 16 cells.
(a) Estimate the cell size for each group.
(b) Find the mean of the three estimates to the nearest µm.
(c) Give one reason why the estimates differ and suggest one way to make the final estimate more reliable.
questions.a: (a) P: 5000/25 = 200 µm; Q: 5000/20 = 250 µm; R: 4000/16 = 250 µm. (b) Mean = (200 + 250 + 250)/3 = 233 µm. (c) Counting is done along one line and cells differ in size, so counts vary a little; repeating the count on several lines or slides and averaging the results gives a more reliable value.
s: Three correct estimates 200, 250 and 250 µm
Mean of 233 µm
A reason for the difference
A way to improve reliability, such as repeating and averaging

questions.q: A school can use a light microscope (10X eyepiece, 40X objective) for all Class 9 practicals. For each task decide whether this microscope is enough or an electron microscope is needed, and justify your decision with a chapter fact or a number: (i) estimating the size of an onion peel cell, (ii) looking at the surface of a Colocasia leaf with its stomata in very fine detail, (iii) seeing a ribosome.
questions.a: (i) The light microscope is enough: Activity 2.1 uses it, and a cell of 200 µm at 400X is easily seen. (ii) Very fine surface detail, as in the book's electron micrograph of the Colocasia leaf, calls for an electron microscope, which uses a beam of electrons and shows detail at the nanometre scale. (iii) A ribosome is an organelle, and most organelles are visible only with an electron microscope, so the light microscope is not enough.
s: Task (i) decided with Activity 2.1 as the reason
Task (ii) decided with the electron-beam, nanometre-scale detail as the reason
Task (iii) decided with organelles needing an electron microscope

questions.q:
Rhea does Activity 2.1 on an onion peel with a microscope that has a 10X eyepiece and a 40X objective. The transparent ruler shows the field of view is 6 mm in diameter. Counting along that diameter in a straight line, she finds 24 cells on the first slide. She prepares two more slides from the same onion and counts 25 cells on the second and 22 cells on the third. The teacher wants one value to put in the class table.
(a) Estimate the cell size from the first slide.
(b) How large, in mm, does one such cell appear under this microscope?
(c) She wants to look at the ribosomes in these cells. Can this microscope show them? Give a reason.
(d) Should she report the first slide's value or an average of all three? Decide, with the numbers.
questions.a: (a) 6 mm = 6000 µm and 6000/24 = 250 µm. (b) Magnification = 10 × 40 = 400X, so 250 × 400 = 100 000 µm = 100 mm. (c) No; ribosomes are organelles, which are mostly visible only with an electron microscope (nanometre scale). (d) The counts give 250, 240 and about 272.7 µm, which differ by about 30 µm, so the average, about 254 µm, is the better report because it reduces the effect of any single miscount.
s: Part (a): 250 µm
Part (b): 400X and 100 mm
Part (c): no, organelles need an electron microscope
Part (d): average about 254 µm preferred, with the spread of the three values as the reason

questions.q:
A museum panel says: 'In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork through a microscope of about 200-300X and named the box-like compartments cells. Today a school microscope with a 10X eyepiece and a 40X objective is standard.' A visitor, Kabir, argues that the panel should say school microscopes show cells better than Hooke's did, and also asks why an eye cannot see what a lens can: two dots drawn 0.06 mm apart on a slide look like one point to him.
(a) What is the total magnification of the school microscope, and how does it compare with the top of Hooke's range?
(b) Why do the two dots 0.06 mm apart look like one point to the unaided eye at 25 cm?
(c) The panel adds that an electron microscope uses 'a brighter beam of light'. Is that correct?
(d) The school can buy either a second light microscope or share time on an electron microscope for the same cost. For a class that only measures onion and cheek cells, which should it choose, and what would it give up?
questions.a: (a) 10 × 40 = 400X, which is 100X more than the 300X top of Hooke's range. (b) The gap of 0.06 mm is below the limit of resolution of the human eye (about 0.1 mm at 25 cm), so the two points appear as one. (c) No; an electron microscope uses a beam of electrons instead of light, and this lets it show structure at the nanometre scale. (d) A second light microscope suits cell-size work (cells of 10-100 µm are seen well at 400X) and lets more students work at once; the school gives up the nanometre-scale detail of organelles that only the electron microscope shows.
s: Part (a): 400X, 100X above 300X
Part (b): 0.06 mm is below the 0.1 mm limit of resolution
Part (c): no, a beam of electrons, not light
Part (d): a reasoned choice that names the trade-off

questions.q: In Activity 2.2 a potato piece of initial weight 25 g is kept in 20 per cent salt solution and weighs 21 g after one hour. What is the percentage change in its weight?
questions.a: A decrease of 16 per cent. The loss is 4 g and 4/25 × 100 = 16, a fall because water left the cells by osmosis.
o: A decrease of 16 per cent
An increase of 16 per cent
A decrease of 19 per cent
A decrease of 4 per cent

questions.q: The solute concentration inside a cheek cell is 0.9 units, and the cell is placed in a solution with 0.4 units of solute outside. Which describes the solution and what happens to the cell?
questions.a: Hypotonic solution; water enters the cell and it swells. Outside concentration is lower than inside, which is the hypotonic case, and water moves toward the more concentrated inside.
o: Hypotonic solution; water enters the cell and it swells
Hypertonic solution; water enters the cell and it swells
Hypotonic solution; water leaves the cell and it shrinks
Isotonic solution; there is no net movement of water

questions.q: Mung bean seeds soaked in water for 12 hours are then kept in a concentrated salt solution. What should be observed?
questions.a: The seeds shrink, as water moves from the seed cells into the solution. Water moves from the dilute region (inside the seeds) to the concentrated region outside, so the seeds lose water.
o: The seeds shrink, as water moves from the seed cells into the solution
The seeds swell more, as salt moves into the seed cells from the solution outside
The seeds stay the same size, as the membrane stops all movement of water
The seeds swell further, as water moves toward the concentrated salt solution

questions.q: A drop of ink is added to a beaker of still water and slowly spreads through it, with no membrane anywhere. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Diffusion is happening but osmosis is not, as no membrane is present. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration even without a membrane; osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane.
o: Diffusion is happening but osmosis is not, as no membrane is present
Osmosis is taking place, since particles of ink move from a higher to a lower concentration
Neither is taking place, since the net movement of particles needs a membrane to occur
Osmosis is taking place, since the ink is dissolving in water and water is involved

questions.q: A model of the cell membrane is built for a cell sitting in water, with water on the outside and the watery cytoplasm on the inside. Which arrangement of the lipid bilayer matches the fluid-mosaic model?
questions.a: Water-attracting heads face outwards and water-repelling tails face inwards. The bilayer has heads outwards and tails inwards, with proteins embedded in it.
o: Water-attracting heads face outwards and water-repelling tails face inwards
Water-attracting heads face inwards and water-repelling tails face outwards, with proteins outside
Water-repelling tails face both the outside and the inside of the cell in the bilayer
A single layer of lipids with all the heads on one side and all the tails on the other

questions.q:
Match each situation (column I) with the process or state it shows (column II).
Column I: 1. Water from damp soil entering a root cell  2. Fragrance of incense spreading through a room  3. A potato piece shrinking in 20 per cent sugar solution  4. A cheek cell in a solution whose solute concentration equals that inside the cell
Column II: a. Osmosis with water moving into cells  b. Diffusion with no membrane involved  c. Osmosis with water moving out of cells  d. Isotonic condition with no net movement of water
questions.a: 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-d. Root cells gain water by osmosis; the fragrance spreads by diffusion in air; the potato loses water in the concentrated solution; equal concentrations make an isotonic condition.

questions.q:
Read the statements about movement across the cell membrane.
Statement 1: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration and can occur even without a membrane.
Statement 2: Osmosis is the movement of solute particles across a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute to a concentrated region.
Statement 3: A cell kept in a solution of higher solute concentration than its own contents loses water.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. The second statement is false: osmosis is the movement of water, not solute, across the membrane.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3
1 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Water from the soil enters the root cells of a plant by osmosis.
Reason (R): Proteins embedded in the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane act like gatekeepers in helping substances pass through.
questions.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both are true, but the proteins' role does not explain osmosis; water enters because root cell contents are more concentrated and the membrane is selectively permeable.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: True or False: Osmosis can take place only in cells that have a cell wall. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. Osmosis needs a selectively permeable membrane, not a cell wall. Cheek cells have no cell wall, yet they shrink considerably in 20 per cent sugar solution because water leaves them by osmosis.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: osmosis needs a selectively permeable membrane; wall-less cheek cells lose water and shrink

questions.q:
In Activity 2.2 the two halves of the potato are cut to roughly equal size and weighed before being placed in the two beakers.
(a) Why is the initial weight recorded?
(b) What passes through the membrane in this activity and what is blocked?
questions.a: (a) The change in weight (final minus initial) shows how much water the piece gained or lost, and equal pieces make the two beakers comparable. (b) Water passes through the cell membrane; the salt or sugar molecules are blocked.
s: Part (a): the difference from the initial weight shows the gain or loss
Part (b): water passes, salt or sugar molecules blocked

questions.q: Differentiate between diffusion and osmosis, giving one example of each from the chapter's activities.
questions.a: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration, even without a membrane (a dye or fragrance spreading). Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane (water entering root cells, or a potato piece swelling in plain water).
s: Diffusion defined with an example
Osmosis defined with an example

questions.q:
Two similar animal cells are placed in different liquids: Cell X in pure water and Cell Y in a concentrated salt solution.
(a) Which liquid is hypotonic to the cell contents?
(b) State the direction of water movement for each cell.
questions.a: (a) Pure water, whose solute concentration is lower than inside the cell. (b) Cell X: water moves into the cell and it swells; Cell Y: water moves out of the cell and it shrinks.
s: Part (a): pure water is hypotonic
Part (b): into X, out of Y

questions.q:
The cell membrane is about 8 nm thick, and 1 nm = 0.000001 mm.
(a) Express 8 nm in mm.
(b) How many such thicknesses laid end to end make 1 µm?
questions.a: (a) 8 × 0.000001 = 0.000008 mm. (b) 1 µm = 1000 nm, so 1000/8 = 125 membrane thicknesses.
s: Part (b): 1000 nm / 8 nm = 125

questions.q:
A potato cup (a hollow scooped in a potato half) stands in a beaker of water. A teaspoon of sugar is put in the hollow of Cup B; nothing is put in Cup A.
(a) After two hours water gathers in the hollow of Cup B. Why?
(b) What does Cup A show?
questions.a: (a) The sugar makes the solution in the hollow more concentrated than the water outside, so water moves into the hollow through the potato cells by osmosis. (b) Cup A is the comparison: with no sugar, no water gathers, so the water in Cup B is due to the sugar.
s: Part (a): water moves toward the concentrated sugar by osmosis
Part (b): Cup A is the comparison without sugar

questions.q: Gauri says, 'In Activity 2.2 the potato piece shrank in the salt solution because salt moved into the cells and made them smaller.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. The membrane lets water move in and out but not the sugar or salt molecules. The piece shrank because water moved out of the cells into the more concentrated solution, which is osmosis.
s: Verdict: no
Salt does not cross the selectively permeable membrane
Shrinking is due to water moving out by osmosis

questions.q: A student reports that a potato piece kept in distilled water became lighter by 2 g after an hour. Show that osmosis cannot be the reason for this loss.
questions.a: Cell contents contain dissolved substances, so the inside is more concentrated than distilled water. By osmosis water moves from the dilute outside to the concentrated inside, so the piece should gain weight. A loss of weight is therefore opposite to osmosis and has some other cause.
s: States that cell contents are more concentrated than distilled water
Water by osmosis would move in so weight would rise
Concludes a loss contradicts osmosis

questions.q: Describe a set-up in which a 40 g potato piece is expected to weigh less after an hour, and say which way water moves. If it ends at 34 g, find the percentage loss.
questions.a: Put the piece in a concentrated (for example 20 per cent) salt or sugar solution. Water moves out of the cells into the concentrated solution by osmosis. The loss is 40 - 34 = 6 g, and 6/40 × 100 = 15 per cent.
s: A concentrated solution used outside
Water moves out by osmosis
Percentage loss of 15 per cent

questions.q:
A researcher keeps two carrots of similar size for 24 hours, one in plain water and one in concentrated salt solution. The carrot in plain water stays stiff and crunchy; the other becomes rubbery and limp.
(a) State the hypothesis the experiment tests.
(b) Suggest two improvements to the experiment.
(c) Explain the two results using osmosis.
questions.a: (a) Carrot cells lose or gain water depending on the concentration of the solution outside. (b) Record the initial and final weights of each carrot, and use several carrots of equal size per beaker and keep the time the same. (c) In plain water, water enters the cells, keeping them firm and the carrot stiff; in concentrated salt solution, water moves out of the cells by osmosis, so the carrot becomes limp.
s: Hypothesis linking water movement to the solution's concentration
Two valid improvements (weights, more carrots or equal sizes)
Plain water: water enters, carrot stays stiff
Salt solution: water leaves by osmosis, carrot goes limp

questions.q: Explain how three features of the cell membrane account for what is seen in Activity 2.2, where a potato piece gains weight in plain water and loses weight in 20 per cent salt solution. Use the fluid-mosaic model, selective permeability and the direction of osmosis.
questions.a: The membrane is a lipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it, and the proteins act like gatekeepers deciding what passes (fluid-mosaic structure). It is selectively permeable: water crosses but salt and sugar molecules do not. Osmosis moves water from the dilute to the concentrated side, so in plain water it enters the cells and the weight rises, while in 20 per cent salt solution it leaves the cells and the weight falls.
s: Structure: lipid bilayer with embedded proteins as gatekeepers
Selective permeability: water passes, salt and sugar blocked
Direction in plain water: water in, weight up
Direction in salt solution: water out, weight down

questions.q:
Deepa packs amla in jars to make pickle. A trial with 10 jars of 5 kg amla each (fruit worth Rs 80 per kg, salt Rs 20 per kg) used three salt amounts: 5 per cent, 10 per cent and 20 per cent of the fruit mass. After 30 days the number of jars that spoiled was 8, 1 and 0 respectively. A taste panel found the 20 per cent pickle too salty to sell.
(a) Which process of the chapter does the pickling rely on?
(b) In a pickle jar, which way does water move in a bacterial cell, and why?
(c) Bacteria have a cell wall. Why does it not stop this movement?
(d) Taking salt cost plus the value of spoiled jars as the loss for the batch of 10 jars, work out the loss for each salt level and advise which level Deepa should use.
questions.a: (a) Osmosis. (b) Water moves out of the bacterial cell, because the salt outside makes the surroundings more concentrated than the cell contents (hypertonic). (c) The cell wall is permeable and lets water pass; the membrane is the selective barrier. (d) 5 per cent: salt Rs 50 + 8 spoiled jars x Rs 400 = Rs 3250; 10 per cent: Rs 100 + Rs 400 = Rs 500; 20 per cent: Rs 200 + 0 = Rs 200 but unsellable. Advise about 10 per cent: the loss is small (Rs 500) and the pickle is sellable, while 20 per cent has a lower loss on paper but cannot be sold.
s: Part (a): osmosis
Part (b): water moves out because the outside is hypertonic
Part (c): the wall is permeable, the membrane controls movement
Part (d): losses 3250, 500 and 200 with the 10 per cent advice and reason

questions.q:
A student places potato pieces of 20 g each in four salt solutions of 0, 5, 10 and 20 per cent for one hour. The final weights are 22.4 g, 20.8 g, 19.6 g and 17.2 g in that order. A cook wants potato slices to keep their size, neither swelling nor shrinking, and has only the 5 per cent and the 10 per cent solutions in the kitchen.
(a) Find the percentage change in the weight of the piece in each solution.
(b) Between which two solutions is the concentration that causes no change?
(c) Explain why the piece in 20 per cent solution lost weight, in terms of osmosis.
(d) Which of the two available solutions should the cook use, and what trade-off does she accept?
questions.a: (a) 0 per cent: +12; 5 per cent: +4; 10 per cent: -2; 20 per cent: -14 (percentage change in weight). (b) Between 5 and 10 per cent, where the change goes from a gain to a loss. (c) The 20 per cent solution is more concentrated than the cell contents, so water moves out of the cells by osmosis. (d) The 10 per cent solution is closer to no change (a 2 per cent loss against a 4 per cent gain), but the slices will still shrink slightly, whereas the 5 per cent solution gives a larger swelling.
s: Part (a): +12, +4, -2, -14 per cent
Part (b): between 5 and 10 per cent
Part (c): water leaves cells toward the more concentrated solution
Part (d): 10 per cent with the small shrinking as the stated trade-off

questions.q: Taking a typical bacterial cell as 5 µm across and a eukaryotic cell as 50 µm across, ___ bacteria laid side by side would stretch across the eukaryotic cell.
A microbiologist reports a cell 3 µm across with a cell wall, its DNA lying free in a region with no membrane around it, and no membrane-bound organelles. Which classification fits?
questions.a: A prokaryotic cell, such as a bacterial cell. A cell with a nucleoid and no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles, and a typical 1-10 µm size, is prokaryotic; having a wall does not make a cell eukaryotic.
o: A prokaryotic cell, such as a bacterial cell
A eukaryotic plant cell, since it has a cell wall
A eukaryotic animal cell, since it contains DNA
A eukaryotic cell, since it is only 3 µm across

questions.q: Rhoeo leaf peel and cheek cells are each put in 20 per cent sugar solution for half an hour. Which observation shows the job of the cell wall?
questions.a: The Rhoeo cells keep their outer boundary while their inner content shrinks away from it. The wall holds the plant cell's shape as the membrane pulls away; cheek cells have no wall, so the whole cell shrinks.
o: The Rhoeo cells keep their outer boundary while their inner content shrinks away from it
The cheek cells keep their outer boundary while their inner contents pull away from it
Both kinds of cell swell, but only the Rhoeo cells burst because of the rigid wall
Both kinds of cell shrink to the same extent, with no difference in their outer boundary

questions.q: A tall sunflower stays upright through a monsoon storm, while a human cheek cell on a slide changes shape easily. Which pair of facts best explains this contrast?
questions.a: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall outside the membrane, and animal cells have no cell wall. The wall gives plants, which cannot move away, a rigid structure against wind and rain; wall-less animal cells can change shape.
o: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall outside the membrane, and animal cells have no cell wall
Plant cells have a cytoskeleton of fine fibres, and animal cells have no cytoskeleton at all
Plant cells have a thicker, rigid cell membrane, and animal cells have only a thin cytoplasm
Plant cells are prokaryotic with a rigid wall, and animal cells are eukaryotic and flexible

questions.q: A cook notes that a cabbage leaf stays firm and that the fibre in it passes through the gut undigested as roughage. Which substance in the leaf cells does the chapter link to this?
questions.a: Cellulose, a carbohydrate made of many glucose units, forming the cell wall. The plant cell wall is mainly cellulose, and the cellulose in our diet acts as roughage.
o: Cellulose, a carbohydrate made of many glucose units, forming the cell wall
Lipids and proteins arranged as a bilayer, forming the cell wall of the cabbage cells
Chlorophyll, a green pigment that forms a firm, rigid cell wall around the cabbage cells
DNA, which forms a rigid wall around the cytoplasm and holds the leaf firm

questions.q: Which of these statements is NOT true of eukaryotic cells?
questions.a: Their genetic material lies in a region called the nucleoid, with no membrane around it. The nucleoid belongs to prokaryotic cells; eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus.
o: Their genetic material lies in a region called the nucleoid, with no membrane around it
They can be unicellular or multicellular, unlike the usually unicellular prokaryotic cells
A typical cell is 10 to 100 µm across, larger than a typical prokaryotic cell
They have a cytoskeleton of fine fibres that gives support and helps cell movement

questions.q: Neha fills Table 2.1 for a bacterial cell. Which row of her entries is correct?
questions.a: Cell wall present; well-defined nucleus absent; nucleoid present; membrane-bound organelles absent. A bacterial cell has a cell wall like plant cells but, being prokaryotic, a nucleoid and no membrane-bound organelles.
o: Cell wall present; well-defined nucleus absent; nucleoid present; membrane-bound organelles absent
Cell wall absent; well-defined nucleus present; nucleoid absent; membrane-bound organelles present
Cell wall present; well-defined nucleus present; nucleoid absent; membrane-bound organelles present
Cell wall absent; well-defined nucleus absent; nucleoid present; membrane-bound organelles absent

questions.q:
Read the statements about the outer covering of cells.
Statement 1: Because the plant cell wall is rigid, no water or dissolved mineral can pass through it.
Statement 2: The cytoskeleton of fine fibres gives eukaryotic cells structural support and helps maintain their shape.
Statement 3: Cell walls are found in plant, fungal and bacterial cells.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. The first is false: the wall is rigid but permeable, so water and some dissolved minerals pass through, which helps roots absorb water.
o: 2 and 3 only
2 only
1 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A bacterial cell is called a prokaryotic cell.
Reason (R): It has no well-defined nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles, and its genetic material lies in a nucleoid.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are true, and the absence of a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles is exactly what defines a prokaryotic cell.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Four cells measure 2 µm, 8 µm, 35 µm and 90 µm across.
(a) Which of them fall in the typical size range of prokaryotic cells?
(b) Why can size alone not be used to be sure that one of them is prokaryotic?
questions.a: (a) 2 µm and 8 µm, which lie within 1-10 µm. (b) The ranges are only typical values; the defining features are the absence of a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, so these must also be checked.
s: Part (a): 2 µm and 8 µm
Part (b): sizes are typical; the nucleus and organelles decide

questions.q:
In 20 per cent sugar solution, the Rhoeo leaf peel cells keep the same outer boundary.
(a) Which structure keeps the boundary unchanged?
(b) What happens to the inner content and to the space between the inner and outer boundaries?
questions.a: (a) The rigid cell wall. (b) The inner content shrinks as the cell membrane pulls away from the wall, so the space between the inner and outer boundaries increases.
s: Part (a): the cell wall
Part (b): contents shrink and the gap increases

questions.q: Imran says, 'Only plant cells have a cell wall.' Is he correct? Give a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: No. Cells of fungi and bacteria also have a cell wall outside the cell membrane, giving protection and structural support, so a wall is not limited to plants.
s: Verdict: not correct
Fungi and bacteria also have a cell wall

questions.q:
The plant cell wall is made mainly of cellulose.
(a) What kind of molecule is cellulose, and what units build it?
(b) What is its use in our diet?
questions.a: (a) Cellulose is a carbohydrate formed by many glucose units linked together. (b) In our diet it acts as roughage and helps digestion.
s: Part (a): a carbohydrate of many linked glucose units
Part (b): roughage that helps digestion

questions.q:
A cell is 60 µm across and has a membrane-bound nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts and a cell wall.
(a) Is it a plant cell or an animal cell?
(b) Is it prokaryotic or eukaryotic? Give one reason.
questions.a: (a) A plant cell, because of the cell wall and chloroplasts. (b) Eukaryotic, because it has a well-defined membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (its 60 µm size is also in the 10-100 µm range).
s: Part (a): plant cell, with the wall and chloroplasts as evidence
Part (b): eukaryotic, with the membrane-bound nucleus or organelles as the reason

questions.q: Tara says, 'The cell wall is there only to protect the plant cell from wind and rain.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. Protection against stresses such as wind and rain is one job, because plants cannot move away. But the wall also helps leaves and flowers stay firm and keep their shape, keeps plants upright, and, being permeable, lets water and some dissolved minerals pass so roots can absorb them.
s: Verdict: partly right
Accepts protection from wind and rain
Adds firmness or shape, and permeability for the roots

questions.q: A student's table for Cell Q ticks both 'well-defined nucleus (genetic material enclosed by a membrane)' and 'primitive nucleus or nucleoid (genetic material without membrane around it)'. Show that both ticks cannot be right for a single cell, and say what a cell with both ticks wrongly entered could actually be.
questions.a: The first row says the genetic material is enclosed by a membrane and the second says it has no membrane around it, so one cell's DNA cannot be both. A cell has either a membrane-bound nucleus (eukaryotic) or a nucleoid (prokaryotic), so one of the ticks must be removed after checking.
s: Quotes the two row definitions, membrane around the DNA and none
Concludes they contradict each other
States that the cell is either eukaryotic or prokaryotic, so one tick goes

questions.q: Sana says, 'Animal cells have no cell wall, so nothing supports their shape.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. Animal cells are eukaryotic, and eukaryotic cells have a cytoskeleton, a network of fine fibres that gives structural support, maintains shape, enables movement and internal transport. The lack of a wall only makes them flexible, which supports the movement of animal tissues.
s: Verdict: no
Names the cytoskeleton as the support and shape-keeper
Notes that the missing wall gives flexibility for movement of tissues

questions.q: Rhoeo leaf peel and cheek cells are mounted, observed, and then treated with 20 per cent sugar solution (Activity 2.3). Explain (a) why the leaf cells look box-shaped and regularly arranged while cheek cells look irregular, (b) what happens to each kind of cell in the sugar solution, and (c) how the cell wall can be rigid and still help the roots take in water.
questions.a: (a) Plant cells have a rigid wall outside the membrane that fixes their shape; cheek cells have no wall and so can change shape. (b) In sugar solution both lose water by osmosis; the leaf cells keep their outer boundary because the wall holds shape while the inner content shrinks away from it, but the cheek cells shrink considerably. (c) The wall is permeable, so water and some dissolved minerals pass through it, and with the selectively permeable membrane this lets roots absorb water and nutrients.
s: Part (a): wall fixes plant cell shape, wall-less cheek cells irregular
Part (b): both lose water by osmosis
Part (b): leaf cell boundary same with contents shrinking, cheek cell shrinks
Part (c): wall is rigid yet permeable to water and some minerals
Part (c): permeable wall and selectively permeable membrane together help roots absorb water

questions.q: Three unlabelled cells are examined. Cell P: 4 µm, cell wall, DNA in a nucleoid, no membrane-bound organelles. Cell Q: 45 µm, cell wall, membrane-bound nucleus, chloroplasts. Cell R: 70 µm, no cell wall, membrane-bound nucleus, mitochondria. Classify each as prokaryotic or eukaryotic and as bacterial, plant or animal, justifying each, and say which cells would keep their outer boundary when placed in a concentrated sugar solution.
questions.a: P is prokaryotic (nucleoid, no membrane-bound organelles, 4 µm is in 1-10 µm) and bacterial. Q is eukaryotic (membrane-bound nucleus, 45 µm is in 10-100 µm) and a plant cell (wall and chloroplasts). R is eukaryotic (membrane-bound nucleus, 70 µm) and an animal cell (no wall). Cells P and Q, which have a cell wall, keep their outer boundary as water leaves; cell R shrinks considerably.
s: P classified as prokaryotic and bacterial with reasons
Q classified as eukaryotic plant cell with reasons
R classified as eukaryotic animal cell with reasons
P and Q keep their boundary because of the wall
R shrinks as it has no wall

questions.q:
A teacher is preparing a demonstration on the cell wall for tomorrow. Three slides have lost their labels. Slide 1 shows box-shaped, regularly arranged cells about 150 µm across; in 20 per cent sugar solution their outer boundary stays the same while the inner content shrinks. Slide 2 shows irregular cells that shrink considerably in the same solution. Slide 3 shows cells only about 3 µm across with no defined nucleus. The field of view of the class microscope is 3 mm in diameter, and pupils must count the cells along it.
(a) Identify the cell types on slide 1 and slide 2.
(b) Explain why slide 1 and slide 2 behave differently in the sugar solution.
(c) What is the region holding the genetic material in the slide 3 cells called, and what kind of cells are they?
(d) Pupils will count cells along the diameter. Work out the count for slide 1 and slide 3, and decide which two slides the teacher should use to show the role of the cell wall.
questions.a: (a) Slide 1: plant cells; slide 2: animal cells. (b) The plant cells have a rigid cell wall that keeps the outer boundary while the membrane pulls away from it; animal cells have no wall and shrink as a whole. (c) The nucleoid; prokaryotic cells. (d) Slide 1: 3000/150 = 20 cells; slide 3: 3000/3 = 1000 cells, too many to count. The teacher should use slides 1 and 2, which show the wall's effect side by side with a countable number of cells; slide 3 would need about 1000 cells counted and does not show a wall effect in the observations given.
s: Part (a): plant cells and animal cells
Part (b): wall holds the boundary, wall-less cells shrink
Part (c): nucleoid, prokaryotic
Part (d): counts 20 and 1000 with slides 1 and 2 chosen for the reason given

questions.q:
Scientists from a Lucknow institute studied the hot springs of Puga Valley in Ladakh, where the organisms are mostly heat-loving bacteria called thermophiles, which are unicellular. A student examines two objects from a sample. Object M is 3 µm across. Object N is 40 µm across, has a membrane-bound nucleus and several organelles, and is found as part of a chain of attached cells.
(a) Is object M likely to be prokaryotic or eukaryotic, and what region would hold its genetic material?
(b) Table 2.2 says eukaryotic cells can be unicellular or multicellular. Can object N's chain of cells be a single bacterium? Give a reason.
(c) How many whole M-sized cells would fit side by side across one cell of N?
(d) The student wants to be certain about M. She can measure its size again or look for a nucleus and organelles with an electron microscope. Which is the better test, and why?
questions.a: (a) Prokaryotic (a thermophile bacterium, 3 µm); the nucleoid. (b) No: object N has a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles, so it is eukaryotic, and bacteria are usually unicellular. (c) 40/3 = 13.3, so 13 whole cells. (d) The electron microscope test; the size ranges (1-10 µm and 10-100 µm) are only typical, whereas a prokaryotic cell is defined by having no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles.
s: Part (a): prokaryotic, nucleoid
Part (b): no, a nucleus and organelles mean eukaryotic
Part (c): 13 whole cells
Part (d): electron microscope check with the 'typical size' reasoning

questions.q: On a slide of onion root tip, a student sees some cells with rod-shaped structures in the nucleus region and others with an entangled mass of threads. Which statement about their DNA is correct?
questions.a: The same DNA in both: chromosomes in cells about to divide, chromatin in the resting cells. Chromatin is organised into chromosomes whenever the cell is about to divide; both are DNA with proteins.
o: The same DNA in both: chromosomes in cells about to divide, chromatin in the resting cells
The rod-shaped cells hold DNA, but the cells with the tangled threads contain no DNA at all, only protein
The rod-shaped cells have a different kind of DNA from the cells with the tangled thread-like mass
Chromosomes are made when a cell finishes dividing, and chromatin when it is about to divide

questions.q: A damaged mature red blood cell in a patient is not repaired by the cell itself and is later replaced by a new one. What is the reason that the cell cannot repair or divide?
questions.a: It has no nucleus, so it lacks what directs repair and division. Mature red blood cells are enucleate; without a nucleus they cannot repair or divide and live only about 120 days.
o: It has no nucleus, so it lacks what directs repair and division
It has two nuclei, which stop each other from working properly
It has no cytoplasm, so there is nothing in the cell to repair or divide
Its DNA is a single circular molecule lying in a region called the nucleoid

questions.q: A student writes about Venter's 2010 experiment: 'The scientists built a completely new living cell from non-living chemicals.' What correction does the chapter support?
questions.a: Only the DNA was synthetic; the cytoplasm and membrane came from an existing living cell. The recipient cell had its own DNA removed and the synthetic DNA inserted into it, so a new cell was not made from scratch.
o: Only the DNA was synthetic; the cytoplasm and membrane came from an existing living cell
The DNA was natural, and only the cytoplasm and the cell membrane were made synthetically
The whole cell was synthetic, but the cell was never able to grow or divide on its own
The recipient cell kept its own DNA in place and received the synthetic DNA as well

questions.q: A chemical blocks the pores in the double-layered nuclear membrane of a cell. Which activity is directly stopped?
questions.a: Movement of ribosomal subunits from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, where they form ribosomes. Subunits made in the nucleolus must leave through the pores to the cytoplasm, where one large and one small subunit assemble.
o: Movement of ribosomal subunits from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, where they form ribosomes
Synthesis of ribosomal subunits inside the nucleolus, which is a dense round body in the nucleus
Organisation of chromatin into rod-shaped chromosomes when the cell is about to divide
Formation of the cell membrane around the cytoplasm from its lipids and proteins in the cell

questions.q: Which statement about chromosomes is false?
questions.a: They are visible as rod-shaped structures in every cell, even when it is not about to divide. Chromosomes show up as rod-shaped structures only when a cell is about to divide; otherwise the DNA is chromatin.
o: They are visible as rod-shaped structures in every cell, even when it is not about to divide
They are composed of DNA and specific proteins, and they carry the information for inheritance of characters
They contain information for the inheritance of characters from parents to the next generation
They form from the entangled chromatin material when the cell is about to divide

questions.q: Mature red blood cells survive about 120 days. If the body keeps a steady number of them, about what percentage of them is replaced each day?
questions.a: About 0.83 per cent. One-hundred-and-twentieth of the cells goes each day, and 100/120 = 0.83.
o: About 0.83 per cent
About 1.2 per cent
About 8.3 per cent
About 0.12 per cent

questions.q:
Match each observation (column I) with the structure it shows (column II).
Column I: 1. A tangled mass of thread-like material in a resting cell  2. Rod-shaped structures seen just before a cell divides  3. A dense round body inside the nucleus where ribosomal subunits are made  4. The region of a bacterium where a single circular DNA molecule lies
Column II: a. Nucleoid  b. Chromatin  c. Nucleolus  d. Chromosomes
questions.a: 1-b, 2-d, 3-c, 4-a. Chromatin is the thread-like mass of a resting cell, chromosomes appear before division, the nucleolus makes ribosomal subunits and the nucleoid holds the bacterial DNA.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the genetic material of cells.
Statement 1: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, so they cannot repair or divide themselves.
Statement 2: In a prokaryotic cell the DNA is a single circular molecule associated with specific proteins.
Statement 3: Chromatin is organised into chromosomes whenever the cell is about to divide.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3. All three match the chapter: the enucleate red cell lives about 120 days, the nucleoid holds a circular DNA with proteins, and chromatin turns into chromosomes before division.
o: 1, 2 and 3
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Chromosomes can be seen as rod-shaped structures in every cell at all times.
Reason (R): Whenever a cell is about to divide, its chromatin material gets organised into chromosomes.
questions.a: A is false but R is true. A is false because a non-dividing cell shows chromatin, an entangled mass of threads. R is true.
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

questions.q: True or False: A bacterial cell whose own DNA has been removed can still grow and divide if synthetic DNA is inserted into it, which shows that DNA controls the structure and activities of a cell.
questions.a: True. In Venter's 2010 experiment, the cell with its DNA removed, but cytoplasm and membrane kept, grew and divided under the instructions of the inserted synthetic DNA.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: the cell followed the synthetic DNA's instructions, so DNA controls its structure and activities

questions.q:
Mature human red blood cells have no nucleus.
(a) State one advantage of having no nucleus.
(b) State one disadvantage and the approximate lifespan that results.
questions.a: (a) There is more space for haemoglobin, so more oxygen can be carried to the body's cells. (b) The cell cannot repair or divide itself, so it survives only about 120 days.
s: Part (a): more space for haemoglobin and oxygen transport
Part (b): cannot repair or divide, about 120 days

questions.q:
A bacterial cell and a human skin cell are compared.
(a) Which of the two has a double-layered membrane with pores around its genetic material?
(b) In which is the DNA a single circular molecule associated with proteins?
questions.a: (a) The human skin cell (eukaryotic nucleus with a double-layered nuclear membrane and pores). (b) The bacterial cell, where the DNA lies in the nucleoid.
s: Part (a): the human skin cell
Part (b): the bacterial cell, in the nucleoid

questions.q:
In Venter's experiment, the DNA of a closely related bacterium was removed and the synthetic copy of a Mycoplasma mycoides DNA was inserted.
(a) Which parts of the recipient cell were kept?
(b) Why is the result not a cell made entirely from scratch?
questions.a: (a) The cytoplasm and the cell membrane (the rest of the cell apart from its DNA). (b) Only the DNA was synthetic; all the other parts were taken from an already existing living cell.
s: Part (a): cytoplasm and cell membrane kept
Part (b): only the DNA was synthetic

questions.q: The nucleolus is a dense round body inside the nucleus. State what is made there, and describe how the product becomes a ribosome.
questions.a: Ribosomal subunits are made in the nucleolus. They leave the nucleus for the cytoplasm, where one large and one small subunit assemble to form a ribosome.
s: Ribosomal subunits are made in the nucleolus
Subunits exit to the cytoplasm and one large and one small subunit assemble

questions.q: Rahul says, 'Having no nucleus lets a mature red blood cell carry more oxygen, but it also means the cell cannot repair or divide.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. Without a nucleus there is more space for haemoglobin, so more oxygen can be transported. The same absence means the cell cannot repair or divide, so its lifespan is short, about 120 days.
s: Verdict: yes
More space for haemoglobin means more oxygen carried
No repair or division, so a short life of about 120 days

questions.q: Kavya says, 'A chromosome is made of DNA alone.' Is she correct? Explain, and state what the functional segments of DNA are called.
questions.a: No. Chromosomes are composed of DNA and specific proteins. DNA molecules carry the genetic information, and the functional segments of DNA are called genes.
s: Verdict: no
Chromosomes are made of DNA and specific proteins
Functional segments of DNA are genes

questions.q: Describe what a student would see under the microscope in a single root-tip cell that is about to divide, and explain how it differs from what she saw a day earlier in the same cell when it was not dividing.
questions.a: In the cell about to divide she would see rod-shaped chromosomes, made of DNA and proteins. A day earlier, in the non-dividing state, the DNA was visible only as an entangled mass of thread-like chromatin. The chromatin has been organised into chromosomes.
s: Rod-shaped chromosomes seen in the dividing cell
Entangled thread-like chromatin earlier
Chromatin organised into chromosomes before division

questions.q: Follow the making of ribosomes. (a) State where the subunits are made and what leaves the nucleus and by what route. (b) State how a ribosome forms. (c) Predict, with a reason, the effect on the formation of ribosomes if the nucleolus of a cell were damaged and the effect if the nuclear pores were blocked.
questions.a: (a) Ribosomal subunits are made in the nucleolus and leave the nucleus through the pores of the double-layered nuclear membrane into the cytoplasm. (b) One large and one small subunit assemble in the cytoplasm to form a ribosome. (c) With a damaged nucleolus, subunits would not be made, so fewer ribosomes form. With blocked pores, the subunits made cannot reach the cytoplasm, so no ribosome can assemble there.
s: Subunits made in the nucleolus
Exit through nuclear pores into the cytoplasm
One large and one small subunit assemble
Damaged nucleolus: no subunits, fewer ribosomes
Blocked pores: subunits cannot reach the cytoplasm

questions.q: Describe the main steps of J. Craig Venter's 2010 experiment and decide whether the headline 'Scientists create a new cell from scratch' is accurate. Give a more accurate headline.
questions.a: The team studied the DNA sequence of Mycoplasma mycoides on a computer and chemically synthesised an exact copy. They took a closely related bacterium, removed its DNA but kept the cytoplasm and cell membrane, and inserted the synthetic DNA. The cell grew and divided following the synthetic DNA, showing that DNA controls a cell's structure and activities. The headline is not accurate, because only the DNA was synthetic and the rest of the cell came from an existing living cell. A better headline: 'Synthetic DNA takes control of a living bacterial cell'.
s: DNA copy synthesised from the studied sequence
Recipient cell emptied of its DNA but cytoplasm and membrane kept, synthetic DNA inserted
Cell grew and divided, showing DNA controls the cell
Judgement that the headline is inaccurate, with the reason
An accurate alternative headline

questions.q:
A hospital laboratory notes that a healthy adult has about 2.5 × 10¹³ mature red blood cells in circulation, and that each such cell survives about 120 days. The lab technician explains to a Class 9 group that these cells have no nucleus.
(a) If the number stays steady, about how many red blood cells must the body replace each day? Give the answer in scientific notation to two significant figures.
(b) Why cannot an existing red blood cell make up for the loss by dividing?
(c) What does the absence of a nucleus give the cell?
(d) A student says the body would do better with nucleated red blood cells that live longer. Using the numbers and the chapter, give one point for and one against.
questions.a: (a) 2.5 × 10¹³ / 120 = 2.1 × 10¹¹ cells per day. (b) Without a nucleus the cell cannot repair or divide itself. (c) More space for haemoglobin, so a larger amount of oxygen is carried to all cells. (d) For: a longer lifespan would mean fewer than 2.1 × 10¹¹ cells needing replacement every day. Against: a nucleus takes space that haemoglobin uses, so each cell would carry less oxygen.
s: Part (a): 2.1 × 10¹¹ per day
Part (b): no nucleus, so no repair or division
Part (c): more space for haemoglobin
Part (d): one valid point for and one against, tied to the numbers and the chapter

questions.q:
A research group repeats the idea of Venter's 2010 work. They read the full DNA sequence of the bacterium Mycoplasma mycoides by computer, chemically synthesise an exact copy and insert it into a closely related bacterium whose own DNA has been removed, but whose cytoplasm and cell membrane are left intact. After insertion, the cell begins to grow and divide, and all the cells formed show the features written in the synthetic DNA. A newspaper reports it as 'life made in a laboratory'.
(a) Which parts of the final cell came from an existing living cell?
(b) What does the outcome tell us about the role of DNA in a cell?
(c) Give one reason the newspaper's report overstates the result.
(d) The group could insert the synthetic DNA either into a cell whose own DNA was removed or into a cell whose own DNA was left in place. Which design gives a clearer conclusion about the synthetic DNA's control, and why?
questions.a: (a) The cytoplasm and the cell membrane. (b) DNA controls the structure and activities of a cell. (c) Only the DNA was synthetic; the rest of the cell was taken from an already existing living cell. (d) Removing the cell's own DNA is clearer: then the only instructions available are the synthetic ones, so the growth and division can be credited to them. If the cell's own DNA stayed, both sets of instructions might act and the result could not be traced to the synthetic DNA alone.
s: Part (a): cytoplasm and cell membrane
Part (b): DNA controls structure and activities
Part (c): only DNA was synthetic
Part (d): own DNA removed, with the reason that only one set of instructions remains

questions.q: Under an electron microscope the ER of a pancreatic gland cell that secretes digestive enzymes looks studded with ribosomes, so it is the ___ endoplasmic reticulum.
questions.a: rough

questions.q: A pancreatic gland cell makes an enzyme that will be secreted outside the cell. Which order of organelles correctly traces the enzyme's path?
questions.a: Ribosomes on the rough ER, then Golgi apparatus, then vesicles that reach the cell membrane. The protein is made at ribosomes on the rough ER, modified and packed by the Golgi apparatus into vesicles, and secreted through the plasma membrane.
o: Ribosomes on the rough ER, then Golgi apparatus, then vesicles that reach the cell membrane
Golgi apparatus, then ribosomes on the rough ER, then lysosomes, then the plasma membrane
Smooth ER, then the nucleolus, then the Golgi apparatus, then vesicles, then the plasma membrane
Lysosomes, then rough ER, then the Golgi apparatus, then vesicles reaching the nucleus

questions.q: Electron micrographs show a cell with a large amount of smooth-surfaced membrane network and almost no ribosomes on it. For which job is this cell most likely specialised?
questions.a: Making and storing fats and hormones. Smooth ER has no ribosomes and is involved in the synthesis and storage of fats and hormones.
o: Making and storing fats and hormones
Making proteins for secretion
Breaking down damaged organelles
Making ribosomal subunits

questions.q: In a cell, worn-out organelles and waste keep piling up in the cytoplasm even though protein manufacture is normal. A fault in which organelle is the most likely cause?
questions.a: Lysosomes, the sacs of enzymes that break down unwanted material. Lysosomes keep the cell clean by breaking down unwanted proteins, carbohydrates, fats and damaged parts.
o: Lysosomes, the sacs of enzymes that break down unwanted material
Golgi apparatus, which packs proteins into vesicles
Rough ER, which makes proteins for secretion
Smooth ER, which stores fats and hormones

questions.q: Enzymes made on the rough ER are to be delivered to form new lysosomes. Which organelle sorts them and packs them into vesicles for this purpose?
questions.a: Golgi apparatus. The Golgi apparatus, the cell's post office, modifies, sorts and packages proteins or lipids into vesicles for transport, secretion or lysosome formation.
o: Golgi apparatus
Smooth ER
Nucleolus
Ribosome

questions.q: Camillo Golgi saw a thread-like network in barn owl nerve cells in 1898, but many scientists doubted it existed. Why was it doubted, and what settled it?
questions.a: Early microscopes could not resolve it clearly; electron microscopy confirmed it decades later. The chapter says the early microscopes could not resolve the structure clearly; the electron microscope confirmed it.
o: Early microscopes could not resolve it clearly; electron microscopy confirmed it decades later
Staining made the network disappear, and later work showed that it was only part of the nucleus
The network was seen only in owl cells, and later work showed that it was present in bacteria
It was mistaken for a lysosome, and later work proved it to be part of the endoplasmic reticulum

questions.q:
Read the statements about cell organelles.
Statement 1: The ER takes part in the synthesis and transport of proteins, fats and some hormones in specialised cells.
Statement 2: Smooth ER has ribosomes attached to its surface and is mainly involved in protein secretion.
Statement 3: Lysosomes are double-membrane-bound organelles that make the subunits of ribosomes.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 only. The second statement describes rough ER, not smooth ER, and the third is false because lysosomes are single membrane-bound sacs of enzymes while ribosomal subunits come from the nucleolus.
o: 1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Pancreatic gland cells, which secrete large amounts of enzyme proteins, have a well-developed rough ER.
Reason (R): The smooth ER is involved in the synthesis and storage of fats and hormones.
questions.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both are true, but the smooth ER's role says nothing about why a protein-secreting cell needs rough ER, whose attached ribosomes make proteins.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
A student examines two cells under an electron microscope. Cell Alpha has ER covered with ribosomes. Cell Beta has ER with a smooth surface.
(a) Which cell makes more protein for secretion?
(b) Which cell is more likely to be storing hormones and fats?
questions.a: (a) Cell Alpha, because rough ER with ribosomes is mainly involved in protein synthesis and secretion. (b) Cell Beta, because smooth ER is involved in the synthesis and storage of fats and hormones.
s: Part (a): cell Alpha (rough ER)
Part (b): cell Beta (smooth ER)

questions.q: Differentiate between rough ER and smooth ER on their appearance under an electron microscope and their main work.
questions.a: Rough ER has ribosomes attached to its surface, so it looks rough, and is mainly involved in protein synthesis and secretion. Smooth ER has no ribosomes, so it looks smooth, and is involved in synthesis and storage of fats and hormones.
s: Rough ER: ribosomes attached, protein synthesis and secretion
Smooth ER: no ribosomes, synthesis and storage of fats and hormones

questions.q:
The Golgi apparatus is called the 'post office' of the cell.
(a) Which three actions on proteins and lipids justify this name?
(b) For what three purposes are the vesicles it makes sent out?
questions.a: (a) It modifies, sorts and packages them. (b) For transport, for secretion, or for lysosome formation.
s: Part (a): modifies, sorts, packages
Part (b): transport, secretion, lysosome formation

questions.q: Aman says, 'Lysosomes are the cell's waste because they are full of unwanted material.' Is he right? Give a reason.
questions.a: No. Lysosomes are sacs filled with enzymes that break down unwanted material and damaged parts, so they clean the cell; the breakdown products are released into the cytoplasm and may be reused.
s: Verdict: not right
Lysosomes hold enzymes that break the waste down, products reused

questions.q:
Golgi used special staining techniques in 1898 to see a thread-like network in barn owl nerve cells.
(a) Why did many scientists doubt his observation?
(b) What was later done to confirm the structure, and what was it named?
questions.a: (a) Early microscopes could not resolve the structure clearly. (b) Observations with the electron microscope confirmed it decades later, and it was named the Golgi apparatus in his honour.
s: Part (a): early microscopes could not resolve it clearly
Part (b): electron microscope confirmed it; named the Golgi apparatus

questions.q: Ritu says, 'Ribosomes make proteins only when they are attached to the endoplasmic reticulum.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: No. Ribosomes may be present freely in the cytoplasm or attached to the ER, and in both places they are the sites of protein synthesis. Attachment to the ER is what makes the ER rough.
s: Verdict: no
Ribosomes can be free in the cytoplasm as well as attached
Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis in both positions

questions.q: Dev says, 'A protein made on the rough ER can be modified and packed by the Golgi apparatus before it leaves the cell.' Is he correct? Explain with the pathway.
questions.a: Yes. The ER and the Golgi apparatus are functionally linked: the protein is made at ribosomes on the rough ER, the Golgi modifies, sorts and packages it into vesicles, and the vesicles carry it to the plasma membrane for secretion.
s: Verdict: yes
Rough ER and ribosomes make the protein
Golgi packages it into vesicles that carry it to the plasma membrane

questions.q: A student states that the smooth ER makes the proteins that are secreted by a gland cell. Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: Proteins are made at ribosomes, which are the sites of protein synthesis. Smooth ER has no ribosomes on its surface, so it cannot be a protein-making site. Protein synthesis and secretion belong to the rough ER, while smooth ER works with fats and hormones.
s: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis
Smooth ER has no ribosomes
Concludes rough ER does protein secretion, smooth ER fats and hormones

questions.q: Trace a digestive enzyme through a pancreatic gland cell from its making to its secretion. Name the organelle used at each stage and state its role.
questions.a: The enzyme, a protein, is made at ribosomes. The ribosomes attached to the rough ER carry out the protein synthesis, and the rough ER helps in its secretion. The Golgi apparatus, which is functionally linked to the ER, modifies, sorts and packages it into vesicles. The vesicles move to the plasma membrane, and the enzyme is secreted from the cell.
s: Ribosomes as the site of protein synthesis
Rough ER with attached ribosomes handling protein synthesis and secretion
Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages
Vesicles carry the product to the plasma membrane
The enzyme is secreted out of the cell

questions.q: Use a school canteen to explain the work of ribosomes, the ER, the Golgi apparatus and the lysosomes. Match each organelle to a part of the canteen's work, and say one way in which the comparison does not hold.
questions.a: Ribosomes are the cooks who make the main item (proteins). The ER is the kitchen's manufacturing and transport line, with the rough part making and passing on the dishes and the smooth part dealing with fats. The Golgi apparatus is the packing and dispatch counter that sorts and packs items into boxes (vesicles). The lysosomes are the cleaning staff, whose enzymes break down waste and damaged things. The comparison fails because a canteen's staff are people and the organelles are not; also, lysosomal breakdown products are reused in the cell, whereas canteen waste is thrown away.
s: Ribosomes matched to making proteins
ER matched to manufacturing and transport of proteins and fats
Golgi matched to modifying, sorting and packaging into vesicles
Lysosomes matched to enzyme-based clean-up
A valid limit of the comparison

questions.q:
Under an electron microscope, a researcher counts ribosomes in a section of two cells. Cell P secretes digestive enzymes: it has 1500 ribosomes, of which 1200 are attached to the ER. Cell Q stores fats and hormones: it has 500 ribosomes, of which 40 are attached to the ER.
(a) What percentage of ribosomes is attached to the ER in each cell?
(b) Which cell has more rough ER, and what does it make?
(c) What does the Golgi apparatus do with the product in cell P?
(d) The researcher must choose one of the two cells to study how fats and hormones are made. Which should she choose and what would she expect to see?
questions.a: (a) Cell P: 1200/1500 = 80 per cent; cell Q: 40/500 = 8 per cent. (b) Cell P, which makes proteins for secretion. (c) It modifies, sorts and packages the proteins into vesicles for transport and secretion. (d) Cell Q, because its ER is largely smooth, the type involved in synthesis and storage of fats and hormones; she would expect a smooth-looking network with few ribosomes.
s: Part (a): 80 per cent and 8 per cent
Part (b): cell P makes protein for secretion
Part (c): Golgi modifies, sorts and packs into vesicles
Part (d): cell Q, with smooth ER and few ribosomes expected

questions.q:
In cell A, the lysosomes can clear 5 damaged organelles or other pieces of waste per hour when working at full strength, but the cell now works at 60 per cent of full strength and makes 80 damaged parts a day. In cell B, the lysosomes also have a full-strength rate of 5 per hour but now work at 40 per cent of full strength, while the cell makes only 50 damaged parts a day. Waste that is not cleared stays in the cell.
(a) How many pieces can the lysosomes of a cell clear in a day at full strength?
(b) For cells A and B, find the number left uncleared each day.
(c) In how many days will 100 uncleared pieces build up in each cell?
(d) Which cell would you examine first, and what trade-off do the numbers show?
questions.a: (a) 5 × 24 = 120 pieces a day. (b) Cell A clears 0.6 × 120 = 72 so 80 - 72 = 8 are left each day; cell B clears 0.4 × 120 = 48 so 50 - 48 = 2 are left. (c) Cell A: 100/8 = 12.5 days; cell B: 100/2 = 50 days. (d) Cell A first, because its waste builds up fastest even though its lysosomes work better (60 per cent) than those of cell B (40 per cent); the speed of build-up depends on both the clearing rate and the amount of waste made.
s: Part (a): 120 pieces a day
Part (b): 8 and 2 left each day
Part (c): 12.5 days and 50 days
Part (d): cell A first, with the trade-off between clearing strength and waste produced

questions.q: A model-maker compares eight small spherical mitochondria, each of radius 1 µm, with one giant sphere that holds the same total volume (radius 2 µm). How do their total surface areas compare?
questions.a: The eight small spheres have twice the surface area of the single large sphere. Eight spheres of radius 1 µm have 8 × 4π × 1² = 32π µm², and the one sphere of radius 2 µm has 4π × 2² = 16π µm², a ratio of 2.
o: The eight small spheres have twice the surface area of the single large sphere
The single large sphere has twice the surface area of the eight small ones
Both have the same surface area because the volume is the same
The eight small spheres have eight times the surface area

questions.q: A ripe tomato is red, while a potato tuber is white and stores starch. Which plastids account for the colour of the tomato and for the starch store of the potato?
questions.a: Chromoplasts for the tomato and leucoplasts for the potato. Chromoplasts carry yellow, orange or red pigments, and leucoplasts are colourless and store food such as starch.
o: Chromoplasts for the tomato and leucoplasts for the potato
Chloroplasts for the tomato and chromoplasts for the potato
Leucoplasts for the tomato and chloroplasts for the potato
Chromoplasts for both, since both store food

questions.q: A money plant on a window sill droops when it is not watered for a week and becomes firm again after watering. The change in which structure mainly explains this?
questions.a: The large central vacuole, which loses and regains water. A vacuole holds water in cell sap and keeps pressure inside the cell; when it loses water the cells become less firm and the plant wilts.
o: The large central vacuole, which loses and regains water
The cell wall, which becomes flexible when dry
The mitochondria, which stop making ATP
The chloroplasts, which store the missing water

questions.q: All the mitochondria are removed from a eukaryotic cell. What is the most likely outcome?
questions.a: The cell can no longer release enough energy as ATP from glucose. Mitochondria are the site where glucose is broken down to release energy stored as ATP, the energy currency used for most cellular activities.
o: The cell can no longer release enough energy as ATP from glucose
The cell can no longer make chlorophyll, which is the pigment needed to absorb sunlight
The cell loses its nucleus and all the DNA that directs its structure and activities
The cell can no longer form a cell membrane around its cytoplasm from lipids and proteins

questions.q: Which feature is NOT shared by mitochondria and chloroplasts?
questions.a: Disc-shaped membrane structures containing chlorophyll. Chlorophyll-bearing discs in a stroma belong to chloroplasts only; both organelles have double membranes, DNA and ribosomes.
o: Disc-shaped membrane structures containing chlorophyll
Being surrounded by two membranes
Having their own DNA
Having their own ribosomes

questions.q:
Match each situation (column I) with the organelle responsible (column II).
Column I: 1. A red hibiscus flower attracts a visiting bee  2. A taro corm holds a store of starch  3. A leaf prepares sugar in sunlight  4. Glucose is broken down to release energy as ATP in a muscle cell
Column II: a. Leucoplast  b. Chloroplast  c. Mitochondrion  d. Chromoplast
questions.a: 1-d, 2-a, 3-b, 4-c. Chromoplasts give bright colours that attract pollinators, leucoplasts store starch, chloroplasts make food by photosynthesis and mitochondria release energy as ATP.

questions.q:
Read the statements about mitochondria, plastids and vacuoles.
Statement 1: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is smooth and porous, and its outer membrane is folded into cristae.
Statement 2: Chromoplasts contain yellow, orange or red pigments that give bright colours to flowers and fruits.
Statement 3: A mature animal cell usually has one large central vacuole, while a mature plant cell has only tiny ones.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 only. The first statement reverses the membranes: the outer membrane is smooth and porous and the inner one is folded into cristae. The third reverses the cells: plants usually have one large central vacuole.
o: 2 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Chloroplasts help a plant cell to make its own food.
Reason (R): Chloroplasts are surrounded by a single membrane and contain no DNA of their own.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. A is true because chlorophyll in the chloroplast absorbs light for photosynthesis. R is false: chloroplasts are double-membrane-bound and have their own DNA and ribosomes.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q: True or False: Mitochondria and plastids depend completely on the nucleus, since they have no DNA or ribosomes of their own.
questions.a: False. Both mitochondria and plastids have their own DNA and ribosomes, so they can make some of their own proteins; these features resemble certain bacteria and hint at a shared evolutionary history with single-celled organisms.
s: Verdict: false
Corrected statement: they have their own DNA and ribosomes and make some of their own proteins

questions.q:
A cell breaks down glucose to release energy.
(a) In which organelle does this happen and what is the process called?
(b) In what form is the energy stored, and what is that molecule called in the chapter's words?
questions.a: (a) In the mitochondria, during cellular respiration. (b) As ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate), which acts as the energy currency of the cell.
s: Part (a): mitochondria and cellular respiration
Part (b): ATP as the energy currency

questions.q: Differentiate between chloroplasts and chromoplasts on the basis of their pigments and what each does for the plant.
questions.a: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll, which absorbs sunlight for making food. Chromoplasts contain yellow, orange or red pigments that give bright colours to flowers and fruits and attract pollinators and fruit-eating animals that help in seed dispersal.
s: Chloroplast: chlorophyll (green), absorbs light for food making
Chromoplast: yellow, orange or red pigments, attract pollinators and seed dispersers

questions.q: Rohit says plastids are absent in plant roots since roots are underground and do not do photosynthesis. Judge his reasoning using the chapter.
questions.a: His reasoning is faulty. Plastids are not only for photosynthesis: leucoplasts, which are colourless, store food such as starch, oils or proteins, for example in potato and taro cells, which are underground parts.
s: Judgement: the reasoning is faulty
Leucoplasts store food (starch), e.g. in potato and taro

questions.q:
A potted plant that is not watered for several days wilts.
(a) Which cell organelle loses water?
(b) Why do the cells then become less firm?
questions.a: (a) The vacuole, which stores water as cell sap. (b) The vacuole maintains pressure inside the cell by storing a large amount of water; when it loses water, the pressure falls and the cell becomes less firm.
s: Part (a): the vacuole
Part (b): less water means less pressure inside the cell

questions.q:
The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is folded into finger-like projections.
(a) What are these projections called?
(b) How do they help the mitochondrion?
questions.a: (a) Cristae. (b) They increase the surface area for chemical reactions and so help energy production.
s: Part (a): cristae
Part (b): more surface area for reactions, helping energy production

questions.q: Meera says, 'Mitochondria make food for the cell, just as chloroplasts do.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: No. Chloroplasts make food (sugars) by photosynthesis in the presence of sunlight. Mitochondria do not make food; they break down glucose and other molecules from food by cellular respiration to release energy stored as ATP.
s: Verdict: no
Chloroplasts make food by photosynthesis
Mitochondria release energy from food as ATP

questions.q: Karan says, 'Mitochondria and plastids both have their own DNA and ribosomes, which suggests they share an evolutionary history with single-celled organisms.' Is he correct? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. Both have their own DNA and ribosomes and can make some of their own proteins, features that are similar to certain bacteria, so the chapter suggests a shared evolutionary history with those single-celled organisms.
s: Verdict: yes
Both have own DNA and ribosomes and make some proteins
These features resemble bacteria, suggesting shared history

questions.q: A drawing of a cell shows a large central vacuole filling most of the cell, several chloroplasts and mitochondria. A student labels it 'animal cell'. Show that this label cannot be right.
