questions.a: A large central vacuole belongs to a mature plant cell; animal cells may have vacuoles but they are small and used for temporary storage. Chloroplasts are plastids, which are organelles of plant cells. The drawing therefore fits a plant cell.
s: Large central vacuole is a mature plant cell feature, animal vacuoles are small
Chloroplasts are plastids found in plant cells
Concludes the drawing shows a plant cell

questions.q: Compare mitochondria and chloroplasts: give two ways in which they are structurally or genetically alike, and three differences in structure or function.
questions.a: Alike: both are surrounded by two membranes, and both have their own DNA and ribosomes, so they make some of their own proteins. Different: the mitochondrion's inner membrane is folded into cristae, but a chloroplast has a semi-fluid stroma with disc-shaped membrane structures holding chlorophyll; a mitochondrion carries out cellular respiration, releasing energy as ATP, while a chloroplast carries out photosynthesis; mitochondria are found in cells generally but chloroplasts are plastids in plant cells, where the sugars and starch they make are stored in the stroma.
s: Alike: two membranes
Alike: own DNA and ribosomes
Difference in structure: cristae against stroma with chlorophyll discs
Difference in function: respiration and ATP against photosynthesis
A third valid difference, such as site or storage

questions.q: A student asks why a plant wilts when it gets too little water and becomes firm again after watering. Answer using the vacuole, the cell wall and osmosis.
questions.a: The central vacuole stores water as cell sap and, by holding a large amount of it, maintains pressure inside the cell, which keeps the plant cell firm. With too little water the vacuole loses water, the cells become less firm and the plant wilts. After watering, water from the soil enters the root cells by osmosis and the vacuoles fill again, restoring the pressure, and the rigid cell wall keeps the cell in its shape.
s: The vacuole stores water in cell sap
Stored water maintains pressure and keeps the cell firm
Too little water: vacuole loses water, cells less firm, plant wilts
Water from the soil enters root cells by osmosis on watering
The wall keeps the shape of the refilled cell

questions.q:
A student models mitochondria for a science exhibition. Model A uses one large sphere of radius 2 cm. Model B uses eight small spheres of radius 1 cm each. Both models hold the same total volume. She wants to show why a cell has many small mitochondria rather than one giant one. Use π = 3.14.
(a) Calculate the total surface area of Model A.
(b) Calculate the total surface area of Model B and the ratio of B to A.
(c) What does the folding of the inner membrane into cristae do to the surface area of a real mitochondrion?
(d) The exhibition judge asks which model supports the idea better and why that matters for ATP production. Give your decision.
questions.a: (a) 4 × 3.14 × 2² = 50.24 cm². (b) 8 × 4 × 3.14 × 1² = 100.48 cm², so the ratio is 100.48/50.24 = 2. (c) The cristae increase the surface area for chemical reactions. (d) Model B: for the same volume it has twice the surface area, and more surface means more area for the reactions that release energy as ATP; the chapter adds that cristae raise the surface area further inside each mitochondrion.
s: Part (a): 50.24 cm²
Part (b): 100.48 cm² and a ratio of 2
Part (c): cristae increase the surface for reactions
Part (d): Model B chosen, with surface area and ATP production as the reason

questions.q:
On a school science day, Class 9 students look at three samples: a spinach leaf peel, a piece of ripe red tomato skin, and a thin slice of potato. They have time to prepare only two slides for a practical on plastids and want the two that best contrast a food-making plastid with a food-storing plastid.
(a) Which kind of plastid gives each sample its main feature: the green leaf, the red skin and the starch store?
(b) Why do red and orange colours in fruits and flowers help the plant?
(c) Which of the three plastids make food and which only store or colour?
(d) Decide which two samples they should use for the planned contrast, and say what is lost by leaving out the third.
questions.a: (a) Spinach: chloroplasts; tomato skin: chromoplasts; potato: leucoplasts. (b) Bright colours attract pollinators and fruit-eating animals that help in seed dispersal. (c) Chloroplasts make food by photosynthesis; leucoplasts store food such as starch; chromoplasts give colour through their pigments. (d) Spinach (food-making chloroplast) and potato (food-storing leucoplast); leaving out the tomato loses the chance to see the pigment-bearing chromoplast and how plastids give colour.
s: Part (a): chloroplast, chromoplast, leucoplast
Part (b): attract pollinators and seed-dispersing animals
Part (c): chloroplast makes food, leucoplast stores, chromoplast colours
Part (d): spinach and potato chosen, with the loss of the chromoplast example stated

questions.q: The body cells of a plant have 18 chromosomes. Each gamete formed from one of these cells by meiosis has ___ chromosomes.
Arun gets a small cut on his knee and it heals in a few days. Which kind of division produced the new skin cells, and why is it the right kind?
questions.a: Mitosis, because it gives two cells genetically identical to the damaged ones. Mitosis is important for growth, repair and maintenance, and each new cell gets the same DNA and chromosome number as the parent.
o: Mitosis, because it gives two cells genetically identical to the damaged ones
Meiosis, because it gives four cells from each skin cell, so the wound fills quickly
Meiosis, because it halves the chromosomes of the skin cells that were damaged
Mitosis, because it gives four cells with half the chromosomes of the parent cell

questions.q: A cell in the testis of a species has 12 chromosomes and divides by meiosis. What does it produce?
questions.a: Four cells, each with 6 chromosomes. The parent cell divides twice in succession to give four daughter cells, each with half the chromosome number.
o: Four cells, each with 6 chromosomes
Two cells, each with 12 chromosomes
Four cells, each with 12 chromosomes
Two cells, each with 6 chromosomes

questions.q: In a species whose body cells have 12 chromosomes, suppose gametes were formed by mitosis. How many chromosomes would the fertilised egg have?
questions.a: 24. Each mitotic gamete would keep all 12 chromosomes, and two such gametes give 12 + 12 = 24 instead of restoring the original number.

questions.q: A laboratory sets up a culture of skin cells. Which set of conditions must it provide?
questions.a: A nutrient-rich medium, suitable temperature, pH and moisture, all under sterile conditions. Cell culture needs nutrients, controlled temperature, pH and moisture, and sterile conditions to keep the culture safe.
o: A nutrient-rich medium, suitable temperature, pH and moisture, all under sterile conditions
Plain water, room temperature, no control of acidity, and an open dish exposed to the air
A nutrient-rich medium, any temperature, strong sunlight, and a dish left open to the air
Soil, sunlight and a sealed container with no moisture, kept at the temperature of the room

questions.q: Which of these cells would NOT divide by meiosis?
questions.a: A skin cell at the edge of a healed cut. Meiosis occurs only in cells of reproductive organs (testes, ovaries, anthers); skin repair uses mitosis.
o: A skin cell at the edge of a healed cut
A cell in the ovary of a female
A cell in the testis of a male
A cell in the anther of a flower

questions.q: A pathologist finds that cells in a patch of tissue have divided without control and formed a lump. An error in which process is the most likely cause?
questions.a: Mitosis. Errors in mitosis lead to uncontrolled cell divisions, which can form tumours and give body cells an abnormal number of chromosomes.
o: Mitosis
Meiosis in the reproductive organs
Fertilisation
Cell culture in a sterile laboratory

questions.q:
Read the statements about cell division.
Statement 1: Mitosis produces four daughter cells that are genetically different from the parent cell.
Statement 2: Meiosis occurs in all body cells, such as skin cells, when they need to be replaced.
Statement 3: Cell culture needs sterile conditions to keep the growing cells safe.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 3 only. The first statement is false because mitosis gives two identical daughter cells, and the second is false because meiosis occurs only in cells of reproductive organs.
o: 3 only
2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Children resemble their parents but are not exactly the same as them.
Reason (R): Gametes formed by meiosis carry half the chromosome number of the parent cell and combine at fertilisation, which creates variations.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are true; meiosis makes gametes that bring variation, and when two gametes combine the original number is restored in a new combination.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
A body cell of an animal has 12 chromosomes.
(a) How many chromosomes does each daughter cell have after mitosis?
(b) How many gametes form from one parent cell by meiosis and how many chromosomes does each have?
questions.a: (a) 12, since mitosis gives daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent. (b) Four gametes, each with 6 chromosomes.
s: Part (a): 12 chromosomes
Part (b): four gametes with 6 chromosomes each

questions.q: Differentiate between mitosis and meiosis on the number of daughter cells formed and the chromosome number in each.
questions.a: Mitosis forms two daughter cells, each with the same chromosome number and DNA as the parent. Meiosis forms four daughter cells in two successive divisions, each with half the chromosome number.
s: Mitosis: two cells with the same chromosome number
Meiosis: four cells with half the chromosome number

questions.q:
A biotechnology unit grows cells outside the body.
(a) Name this technique and two conditions needed to keep it safe.
(b) Give two uses of the technique.
questions.a: (a) Cell culture; a sterile setting and the right temperature (also pH and moisture, with a nutrient-rich medium). (b) Studying how cells work and producing biochemicals, food, medicines or vaccines.
s: Part (a): cell culture with two correct conditions
Part (b): two valid uses

questions.q: Divya says, 'A child grows taller only because each cell of her body gets bigger.' Judge this using the chapter.
questions.a: The statement is wrong. Cells can grow only up to a certain size, so growth of the body happens because cells divide to form new cells.
s: Judgement: wrong
Cells grow to a limit; growth comes from cell division

questions.q:
Errors can occur in cell division.
(a) State two possible results of an error in mitosis.
(b) State two possible results of an error in meiosis.
questions.a: (a) Uncontrolled cell division leading to tumours, and an abnormal number of chromosomes in body cells. (b) Any two of: genetic disorders, developmental problems or distinctive physical features, early pregnancy loss, reduced fertility.
s: Part (a): two results of an error in mitosis
Part (b): two results of an error in meiosis

questions.q: Ravi says, 'If skin cells divided by meiosis, a cut would heal faster because four cells form from each cell instead of two.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: No. Meiosis occurs only in the cells of reproductive organs, and its four daughter cells have half the chromosome number, so they are not copies of the skin cells. Skin repair needs mitosis, which gives genetically identical cells with the same chromosome number.
s: Verdict: no
Meiosis occurs only in reproductive organs and gives half-chromosome cells
Repair needs the identical cells that mitosis makes

questions.q: Isha says, 'Mitosis is needed only for growth.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. Mitosis is needed for normal growth, but it is also important for repair, maintenance of the body and asexual reproduction, so the word 'only' makes the claim wrong.
s: Verdict: partly right
Accepts growth
Adds repair, maintenance or asexual reproduction

questions.q: A student reports that a body cell with 12 chromosomes divided by meiosis and one of the daughter cells had 12 chromosomes. Show that this cannot be a result of normal meiosis.
questions.a: In meiosis the first division reduces the number of chromosomes in each daughter cell to half and the second is similar to mitosis, so all four daughter cells have half the parent number. Half of 12 is 6, so a normal daughter cell has 6 chromosomes. A cell with 12 would be abnormal.
s: States that meiosis halves the chromosome number
Calculates 12/2 = 6
Concludes 12 is abnormal

questions.q: Compare mitosis and meiosis in a table-like answer. Include where each takes place, the number of divisions, the number and type of daughter cells, the chromosome number in daughter cells and the main purpose.
questions.a: Mitosis: takes place in body cells; one division; two genetically identical daughter cells; same chromosome number as the parent; purpose is growth, repair, maintenance and asexual reproduction. Meiosis: takes place only in cells of reproductive organs (testes, ovaries, anthers); two successive divisions; four daughter cells (gametes); half the chromosome number; purpose is sexual reproduction, creating variation.
s: Site of each division
Number of divisions
Number and type of daughter cells
Chromosome number in daughter cells
Purpose of each

questions.q: Suppose a species whose body cells have 12 chromosomes made gametes by mitosis, not meiosis. Work out the chromosome number of the fertilised egg in each of three successive generations and explain whether this could continue.
questions.a: The first generation egg has 12 + 12 = 24 chromosomes. In the next generation the body cells have 24, so the gametes would have 24 each and the egg 48. In the third generation the egg would have 96. The number would double every generation. This could not continue, since the chromosome number must stay constant; meiosis halves the number in gametes, so fertilisation restores the original number instead of doubling it.
s: First generation egg has 24 chromosomes
Second generation egg has 48 chromosomes
Third generation egg has 96 chromosomes
Number doubles every generation so the system cannot continue
Meiosis halves the number so fertilisation restores it

questions.q:
A biotechnology lab grows skin cells in culture. A culture starts with 1000 cells and every cell divides by mitosis once every 24 hours, so the number doubles each day. The lab needs at least 10 lakh (1 000 000) cells for a vaccine batch. Starter cells cost Rs 40 per 1000 cells, and each day in the incubator costs Rs 500. The lab can choose to start with 1000, 5000, 20 000 or 100 000 cells, and it counts the days needed to reach 10 lakh cells.
(a) How many cells are present after 5 days from a start of 1000?
(b) Why are the daughter cells in this culture all identical?
(c) Why must the culture be kept sterile?
(d) Which starting number gives the lowest total cost (starter cells plus incubator days) for reaching 10 lakh cells?
questions.a: (a) 1000 × 2⁵ = 32 000 cells. (b) Mitosis gives two genetically identical daughter cells with the same DNA as the parent. (c) To keep the culture safe from contamination that would spoil the growth of the cells. (d) 1000 start: 10 days, Rs 40 + Rs 5000 = Rs 5040; 5000 start: 8 days, Rs 200 + Rs 4000 = Rs 4200; 20 000 start: 6 days, Rs 800 + Rs 3000 = Rs 3800; 100 000 start: 4 days, Rs 4000 + Rs 2000 = Rs 6000. The lowest cost is a start of 20 000 cells (Rs 3800), a balance between paying for starter cells and paying for days.
s: Part (a): 32 000 cells
Part (b): mitosis gives identical cells
Part (c): sterile conditions keep the culture safe
Part (d): the four totals and the choice of 20 000 cells

questions.q:
A plant breeder studies pollen formation in the anthers of a flowering plant whose body cells have 14 chromosomes. In a sample, 200 cells of the anther start meiosis. At the end, she finds that 188 of the 200 cells formed pollen grains normally, and the rest showed an error. A seed company will accept a batch only if at least 95 per cent of such cells divide normally.
(a) How many pollen grains, and how many chromosomes in each, come from the 188 normal cells?
(b) If a pollen grain with 14 chromosomes fused with an egg cell formed normally, how many chromosomes would the fertilised cell have?
(c) Name two possible results of a fault in meiosis.
(d) Should the company reject the batch at once or test a bigger sample? Decide, using the numbers.
questions.a: (a) 188 × 4 = 752 pollen grains, each with 7 chromosomes. (b) The egg cell has 7 chromosomes, so the fertilised cell has 14 + 7 = 21, not the original 14. (c) Any two of: genetic disorders, developmental problems, early pregnancy loss, reduced fertility. (d) 188/200 = 94 per cent, only one percentage point below the 95 per cent rule, and the sample is small; the better decision is to test a bigger sample before rejecting, though rejecting avoids passing on faulty cells if the larger sample also stays under 95 per cent.
s: Part (a): 752 grains with 7 chromosomes
Part (b): 21 chromosomes
Part (c): two results of meiotic error

questions.q:
In a laboratory, 500 animal cells are placed in each dish. Normal cells divide once every 20 hours until they form a single layer that covers the dish; this layer holds 64 000 cells, and then they stop. Cancer cells in another dish keep dividing at the same rate without stopping. A third dish, starting with 500 cells of unknown type, shows 150 000 cells after 200 hours.
(a) How many hours does a normal dish need to reach 64 000 cells?
(b) How many cancer cells will the cancer dish hold after 200 hours?
(c) Which feature of normal cells explains why their number stops at 64 000?
(d) How should the lab classify the third dish? Decide, and say what more evidence it needs.
questions.a: (a) 64 000/500 = 128 = 2⁷, so 7 doublings of 20 hours each, which is 140 hours. (b) 200/20 = 10 doublings, so 500 × 2¹⁰ = 512 000 cells (512 000). (c) Contact inhibition, which stops division when cells touch neighbours. (d) 150 000 is above the 64 000 a normal dish holds, so contact inhibition seems partly lost, but it is below the 512 000 that unchecked growth would give, so the dish cannot be called cancer from the count alone; the lab needs more evidence, such as whether the cells form tumours that invade, before classifying it.
s: Part (a): 140 hours
Part (b): 512 000 cells
Part (c): contact inhibition
Part (d): in between 64 000 and 512 000, suspect but more evidence needed

questions.q:
A nursery wants to raise young plants by tissue culture, using the idea that a mature plant cell can develop into a whole plant. One batch uses 25 leaf pieces, each of which gives 40 plantlets. In a batch, 15 per cent of the plantlets fail. The cost of the batch is Rs 9000, and a one-time setup of Rs 3000 is needed before the first batch. A supplier sells ready seedlings at Rs 15 each.
(a) Who proposed this property of plant cells, in which year, and what is it called?
(b) How many healthy plantlets does one batch give?
(c) Find the cost per healthy plantlet in the first batch and in a later batch.
(d) The nursery thinks the failure rate may rise to 30 per cent. Should it use tissue culture for the first batch? Decide, using your numbers.
questions.a: (a) Gottlieb Haberlandt, in 1902, called totipotency. (b) 25 × 40 = 1000 plantlets, and 85 per cent of them is 850 healthy plantlets. (c) First batch: (9000 + 3000)/850 = Rs 14.1 each; later batch: 9000/850 = Rs 10.6 each. (d) At 30 per cent failure only 700 are healthy and the first batch costs 12 000/700 = Rs 17.1 each, more than the supplier's Rs 15; at 15 per cent it is only just cheaper (Rs 14.1). So the first batch is worthwhile only if the failure rate stays near 15 per cent, and a later batch (Rs 12.9 even at 30 per cent failure) is cheaper in either case.
s: Part (a): Haberlandt, 1902, totipotency
Part (b): 850 healthy plantlets
Part (c): Rs 14.1 and Rs 10.6
Part (d): Rs 17.1 at 30 per cent failure and a reasoned decision
